zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Only the supplied page subset was consulted; its headwords are lexical evidence, not a replacement transcription. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Corrections and English review notes are by the external AI reviewer identified in result.json.

lines.note: Ryosoku denotes money, here copper cash or coins. The gloss reads moedas, not mordas. The worn synonym is read Ieni, with consonantal capital I for zeni, a form discussed in the supplied historical-language notes; its initial is a straight serifed stroke, not a secure long-s hook. The damaged initial remains a nonblocking uncertainty.
The entry equates ryo with sunadori and covers both hunting and fishing. The circumflex on Reô is retained as a graphic distinction, not normalized from the modern word.
Tabino michi identifies the road or course of a journey. The final vowel of michi is i, not OCR michu; the Portuguese relative clause continues below.

runs.text: faz andando por fora, ou peregrinando.

lines.note: Completes the description of a route taken while away from home or travelling as a pilgrim. It belongs to Reoto, not to a new entry.

Satori and uru explain gaining understanding. A faint raised mark above the first o is read as a circumflex, supported on reinspection by its position; the NINJAL headword also has Reôtocu, but does not establish the mark by itself. The Portuguese conſidera- continues below.
Completes consideração and adds discursive reasoning as the other explanation of understanding. The printed word is diſcurſo, not the OCR's shortened diſcuſo.

The gloss defines a hunter or fisherman. The e and vowel mark in the damaged headword are weak; Reôxi is the chosen reading, matching the preceding hunting entry. The pale mark before Caçador is not a secure printed paragraph sign.
This separate homographic entry means paper, not a hunter. Papel is clearly legible, correcting Paprl; the mark on the headword is read as a circumflex.

The first sense is two places; the following row adds two people. The Japanese gloss corresponds to futa tokoro, but the internal letters and spacing of the short printed form require retention rather than automatic expansion.
Adds the personal sense, two people, to the preceding two-place expression. The joined double-s type is preserved in the project's existing ß representation.

runs.text: Lugar, onde ſe hum acha fora de

lines.note: Defines the place where someone finds himself away from home. Lugar and acha restore the words visible in the scan; the unaccented headword is distinct from the adjacent long-vowel forms.
Completes fora de sua casa, specifying that the place is outside one's own home. This short continuation is a full physical row.

runs.text: Terras, ou renda propria dalgum ſe-

lines.note: This entry concerns a lord's own lands or income. The headword's circumflex is compared with the repeated goreôxo below; the Portuguese ſe- begins senhor across the line break.

runs.text: nhor, que tem reſeruada pera ſeu vſo, &

lines.note: Completes senhor and explains that the property is reserved for his own use. The ending of vſo is o, not the OCR's a.
Completes the lord's personal use and expenditure, then gives the imperial example Dairi goreôxo. The following gloss describes income or lands belonging directly to the sovereign.

runs.text: terras proprias do Rey. i, que não tem repar-

lines.note: The royal lands are explained as those not distributed to retainers. Rey belongs wholly to the italic Portuguese gloss; repar- begins repartidas on the next row.
Completes repartidas aos criados: the royal property has not been allotted to the sovereign's servants or retainers.
Futakusa explains two kinds of things. The caron on Reǒxu is distinct from the circumflex in several nearby Reô entries.
The example thanks someone for giving two things. Catajiqenai expresses gratitude; Des- begins the Portuguese past-tense translation on the next line.

runs.text: teme duas couſas, agradeçoue lo muito.

lines.note: Completes the statement that two things were given and are gratefully acknowledged. The historical wording and separation in agradeçoue lo are retained without modernizing the pronouns.
Tabi no yadori identifies lodging while travelling. The Portuguese offers an inn as the first equivalent and continues with another lodging term below.
Adds accommodation away from home, completing the travel-lodging definition. The row is not a separate headword.

The Japanese explanation means far distant, matching grande distancia. The middle letters of touoi are worn; the distance gloss supplies context but does not justify silently regularizing the printed sequence.
Reôyen no kuni exemplifies a very distant country. The italic Vt introduces the example, and diſtã- carries its abbreviation mark into the divided Portuguese adjective.
Completes the adjective distante and supplies longe as the alternative: far away. The line belongs to the distant-country example.

runs.text: Curar doença, & ter cuidado de ſua

lines.note: The entry combines treatment of illness with care of one's health. The two different marks in Reôyǒ are visible and are not made uniform.
Completes the health definition and begins an example of someone accomplished in both treatment and health preservation. Tat- continues as tatxa on the next physical row.
Xa completes the Japanese description of an accomplished practitioner. The Portuguese calls him a skilful and celebrated physician; afamado has f, not the OCR's long s.
Specifies the physician's two accomplishments: curing ailments and preserving health at the same time. Infirmidades is retained as printed.
Completes juntamente and its object, health. The tight printed attachment in aſaude is preserved rather than expanded from modern word spacing.
Koyomi identifies the calendar. The gloss enumerates days and months before continuing to the year below.
Finishes the calendar sense and introduces another: the science of observing celestial objects. Its purpose is specified by the following two rows.

runs.text: as eſtrellas, ou planetas, pera ſaber da vida,

lines.note: The objects observed are stars or planets, to learn about a person's life. Eſtrellas and pera are supported by the visible type rather than the OCR's eſtellaes and para.
Adds each individual's fortune, making the preceding celestial science explicitly divinatory in this gloss.
Reki wo manabu means studying calendrical knowledge; the Portuguese identifies it here as the study of astrology. Its aſ- continues below.
Completes astrologia, the Portuguese subject of study. The short row is preserved rather than joined to the preceding line.
Akirakani shiretaru koto explains something clearly known. The Portuguese noun at the end is completed by its description on the next row.
Describes the thing as manifest and beyond doubt. Manifeſta contains f before e; replacing it with long s would obscure the Portuguese word.

The entry refers back to the evident or unmistakable sense. Although the expected adjective and NINJAL entry have Reqijenna, the second suffix letter in this impression opens upward and is read u. The aligned draft's anomalous Reqijenua is therefore retained rather than silently regularized; wear makes that distinction nonblockingly uncertain.
Gives the corresponding adverb, meaning clearly or manifestly. Aduer. is the italic grammatical label, not Japanese text.
Hi wo heru is explained as the passing or completion of a day. The Portuguese infinitive is acabarſe, with the r present, rather than OCR acaba ſe.
Toshi wo heru concerns a year passing. The final upright S. marks written usage and is not part of the italic definition. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
The first sense of rekireki is numerous things plainly apparent. The description of their arrangement continues below.

runs.text: por ordem. ¶ Item, permet. Muitas peſ-

lines.note: Completes the ordered, evident arrangement and introduces a transferred sense concerning distinguished people. The printed permet. remains unexpanded.
Completes peſſoas and describes them as honourable and principal people. The next clause qualifies whether the expression must refer to more than one person.

runs.text: ſe toma por hũa ſoo. i, do numero das peßo-

lines.note: Explains that the expression can also designate a single person belonging to that distinguished class. Peßo- continues on the following physical row.

Completes the description of grave or exceptional people and begins rekireki no gakushō. Graues, not eraues, fits the visible initial and the preceding description; ga- continues at the top of column 2.
Cuxǒ completes ga-cuxǒ from column 1, referring to distinguished scholars. Letrados supplies the missing r in the OCR; Dǒri starts a second example involving reasons.
Dōri rekirekitari is explained as there being many clear reasons. The Japanese predicate and the Portuguese plural belong to the same example.

runs.text: & de que ſe não pode duuidar.

lines.note: Completes the description of reasons that cannot be doubted. Duuidar, not ducidar, is supported by the paired u forms in the scan.

runs.text: Numero de tempos, ou de annos ja

lines.note: Rekisū concerns the number or reckoning of elapsed periods or years. The vowel with caron after ſ does not require the OCR's extra i; annos replaces the misread onnos.
Completes the elapsed-years sense and introduces astronomy as a second sense. The visible tr sequence gives Aſtronomia, not Aſtionomia.
Adds calculation or counting to the preceding astronomical art. This completes Reqiſǔ before the next independent headword.
Rekitai denotes past ages in succession. Foram is the Portuguese verb, not OCR ſcram; the final adjective continues below.
Completes sucessivamente and explains that those ages followed one another continuously.
Koyomi tsukuru hito identifies the person who makes the calendar. Both the initial R of Reqixa and the m of Coyomi are recoverable from the scan.

runs.text: que faz o calendario, ou reportorio.

lines.note: Defines the astrologer as a maker of calendars or an almanac. Reportorio is retained as the printed historical form.

runs.text: Liuro por onde ſe aprende a arte de

lines.note: This entry is a book from which the astronomical art can be learned. The Portuguese phrase requires its subject on the next row.
Completes the title of the art taught by the book: astronomy. Its capital and italic type are retained.
Mairi tsuranaru describes people coming together in a group. The headword begins R, not B; jũ- starts the Portuguese juntos across the line break.

runs.text: tos como apedir, ou propor algũa couſa, &c.

lines.note: The group comes together to petition or propose something. Tos completes juntos; the tightly printed apedir is not modernized by inserting a space.
The example describes presenting a matter with many people assembled. Junta- begins the Portuguese adverb corresponding to the collective action.
Completes juntamente falar: speaking together as a group. This is the end of the Retſan example.
Za ni tsuranaru concerns sitting in an ordered gathering. The scan gives Retza and Zani, correcting the OCR's Retea and Zuni.
Specifies that many people are seated in order. This finishes the entry before the internal R-before-I heading.
Ri is equated with kotowari and defined as reason or reasoning. The enlarged R belongs to this headword and extends beside the next line; the OCR split it into unrelated fragments.
Ri ni oruru means yielding to or being defeated by reason. The supposed initial N in the draft was part of the enlarged R above, not body text on this row.
Finishes the idea of submitting to reason, then begins ri ni kakawarazu. The visible r before the final a corrects cacauata-.

runs.text: Não ter de ver com arezão. ¶

lines.note: Zu completes kakawarazu, having no connection with reason. Ri wo begins the next example; the historical spacing of arezão remains unchanged.
Ri wo maguru is bending or distorting reason. The next example begins ri ni tsumaru, whose final syllable is on the following row.
Completes tsumaru and the sense of being brought to a decisive conclusion by reason. Another ri wo example begins at the right edge.

runs.text: Dizer todas as rezoens, ou arre-

lines.note: Tsukusu completes ri wo tsukusu: setting out all the reasons. The Portuguese arre- begins the parallel verbal gloss on the next row.
Completes arrazoar, describing full and extended reasoning. Diffuſamente has the i omitted by OCR; the next example begins ri ni hazzururu.
Gives hazzururu and moruru as alternatives for departing from reason. The Latin l means 'or' and remains separate from the Japanese verbs.
This separate ri entry concerns painful bowel movements. Ri wo wazzurō is the example of suffering from that complaint; its final syllable continues below.
Completes wazzurō and the explanation of being ill with this bowel complaint. The medical wording is transcribed as a historical gloss, not offered as a diagnosis.
Ri is equated with toku and defined as benefit or gain. The short synonym reads Tocu rather than the OCR's marked Tǒcǒ; ri wo begins the example below.
Ri wo uru means obtaining profit; ri ni fukeru introduces excessive absorption in gain. The next row explains that second example.

runs.text: Ser muito cubiçoſo, ou amigo de ſeu proueito.

lines.note: Defines the excessive pursuit of profit as being very covetous or devoted to one's own advantage.
Katsu koto supplies a separate victory sense of ri. The example Riuo is wholly roman Japanese, not partly italic as in the OCR draft.
Ri wo ushinō means losing victory, while ri wo uru means winning it. The Portuguese is victoria, not the OCR's victeria.

Completes the winning example and states that Xôri is more commonly used. The embedded word has sloping lowercase ôri, contrasting with the upright repeated example below; the aligned draft's roman capital X is retained. The whole-word font assignment is a nonblocking typography caveat, not a reason to normalize the word.
Shōri wo uru exemplifies the preferred expression for achieving victory. Its circumflex agrees with the preceding embedded form.
Ryaku is an abridgment or summary; ryaku suru means to abridge. A- begins the divided Portuguese infinitive below.

Breuiar completes the verbal gloss. The separate far-right '(qualquer couſa.' is physically on this row but completes the next entry's 'em'; its position and opening mark are preserved rather than reordered.
Ryakugi denotes an abbreviated thing or a summary in any subject. The words completing em are displaced to the right end of the preceding physical line.
Gives the adjectival form with the same abridgment sense. Idem refers back to Riacugui.
Gives the corresponding adverb, meaning in abridged form. Adu. is the italic grammatical abbreviation.
Ribai is glossed by onzena, interest-taking or usury. The example describes carrying on that activity, with its Portuguese explanation continuing below.

runs.text: officio de onzeneiro, ou ganhar à onzena.

lines.note: Completes the example as acting as a moneylender or earning by interest. The historical financial vocabulary is retained without imposing a numerical rate.
Names the person engaged in that interest-taking activity. The Portuguese agent noun directly matches the preceding definition.
Hanare wakaruru explains separation or parting. The gloss continues with separação at the start of f418; the same word appears here only as the bottom catchword.
